tagline.text: A Ramsar wetland on the Agusan River and a Manobo floating village

location.label: Location
location.text: Bunawan and Loreto area, Agusan del Sur (Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000–6,000 (boat, fees and lodging combined; varies with group size)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Butuan Airport (BXU) or Francisco Bangoy International Airport, Davao (DVO)

children.text: Agusan Marsh is one of the largest freshwater wetlands in the Philippines, covering about 14,836 hectares, and has been a Ramsar site since 1999. The classic trip is a 2-day, 1-night boat journey from Bunawan to a Manobo floating village, its lake and its migratory birds.
Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary is a mosaic of lakes, swamps and channels spread across the Agusan River basin in Agusan del Sur, in northeastern Mindanao. It covers about
14,836 hectares

, was declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1996 and was listed as Ramsar Site No. 1009 in November 1999. It became an ASEAN Heritage Park in 2018, and in November 2025 it was added to the East Asian–Australasian Flyway Partnership (EAAFP) flyway site network (EAAF 159) at the 12th Meeting of Partners in Mactan, Cebu. The sanctuary spans six municipalities: Bunawan, La Paz, Loreto, Rosario, San Francisco and Talacogon.

The appeal here is not fancy facilities but water, people and birds. In the wet season the river overflows and floods the forest and grassland, and Manobo families live in bamboo and nipa houses built on logs that rise and fall with the water. Gliding slowly across a lake covered in lotus and water hyacinth in a small motorized boat or canoe feels unlike anywhere else in the Philippines. The Philippine duck, great egret and whiskered tern are among the birds mentioned, and more than 200 bird species are said to use the marsh. Travel accounts also mention mudfish, tilapia and gourami, and describe lotus, water hyacinth and water lilies as common. The soft-shelled turtle known as dinata and the golden-crowned flying fox are presented as emblematic wildlife, but seeing them depends on luck, so keep expectations modest and enjoy the scenery itself.
The most visited spot is the
Lake Panlabuhan floating village
in Poblacion, Loreto. It is about
2 hours

by boat from the wharf near the Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) in Bunawan, and the provincial tourism office lists cultural immersion with the Manobo community, kayaking, birdwatching, fishing, photography and lake hopping as activities. The provincial program includes the Manobo welcome and permission ritual known as panawagtawag, so go with the mindset of a guest who has been given permission to visit, not a spectator. The journey to the lake village is itself a highlight, so do not rush on the boat; bring binoculars and a telephoto lens to get much closer to the birds.

Getting there is not easy. You fly from Manila to Butuan or Davao, travel overland to Bunawan, and then continue by boat. That is why a 2-day, 1-night trip is more realistic than a day trip, and contacting the management office in advance to arrange your schedule is the most important preparation. Rather than expecting city sightseeing or a beach holiday, approach this as a trip to meet quiet nature and an indigenous community with respect. The fees and schedules here are compiled by comparing the provincial tourism page with travel blogs, and sanctuary rules and prices can change. Please check the latest announcements with PAMO or the Agusan del Sur provincial tourism office before you leave.

This lake village is home to Manobo floating houses built on logs. In the provincial tourism program, a welcome ritual, lunch and an evening boat tour follow your arrival, and spending the night with the community is the core experience here.
The provincial 2-day, 1-night itinerary includes a village and lake boat tour and sunset at around
, then sunrise and an early boat ride the next day at
. Sunrise seen from just above the water is considered the most photogenic moment of the trip.

More than 200 bird species are known to live in or pass through the sanctuary. The Philippine duck, great egret and whiskered tern are mentioned, and several travel accounts say birdwatching is best in
November–March
, when migratory birds arrive.

Travel accounts describe the Manobo community as Christian yet maintaining many traditional customs, and as welcoming to visitors. Because you go through the panawagtawag welcome ritual, you should follow the village's rules and photography etiquette.
The provincial tourism office lists lake hopping by bauto (a small canoe) as a separate fee item. Paddling among lotus and water plants lets you see waterbirds and fishers up close.

Lolong, a saltwater crocodile of about 6.17 m caught in the Agusan River in Bunawan in 2011, entered Guinness records and died in February 2013. Crocodiles are said to still live in the marsh, but sightings are reported to be rare.

blocks.title: Lake Himbang in Talacogon and the La Paz bird lake

children.text: Some sources say you can also see the lake and floating huts by pumpboat or canoe at Lake Himbang in Talacogon, and describe Lake Mambagongon in La Paz as a gathering place for migratory birds. Access and fees need to be confirmed locally.

items.title: 2-day, 1-night Lake Panlabuhan floating village route
items.subtitle: A standard route based on the provincial tourism itinerary (times are as published; confirm locally)

children.text: Arrive at the Bunawan PAMO (IPAS Complex), register and attend the environmental orientation. It is safer to contact them before you arrive.
Take a pumpboat from the wharf along the marsh waterways to Lake Panlabuhan. The trip is described as taking about
2 hours
by boat.
You are welcomed by the Manobo community and go through the panawagtawag permission ritual.
Have lunch of local dishes with the community.
Take a boat tour of the village and lake, watch birds, take photos and see the sunset.
Have dinner, then spend the evening interacting with the community from around
and stay overnight in the village.

sunrise and early boat ride,

items.title: Day exploration from Butuan
items.subtitle: A realistic alternative for those short on time

children.text: Leave early from Butuan by bus or van toward Bunawan. Travel time and frequency must be confirmed locally.
Register at the Bunawan PAMO and ask whether boat rental is available and at what price.
Look around the nearby waterways and wharf area, and confirm boat and transport times for the return.
The boat travel to Panlabuhan and back is long, so a day trip is not recommended. Plan a 2-day, 1-night stay if you can.
Flying from Manila to Butuan (BXU) or Davao (DVO) is the most common way. Check airline announcements for routes and frequencies.
Some travel accounts say the overland trip is long from Davao and relatively closer from Butuan. Choose based on fares and your schedule.

items.title: From Butuan or Davao to Bunawan

children.text: The provincial tourism office tells visitors to take a bus or van from Butuan or Davao to the Bunawan terminal. Some travel accounts give about 3 hours from Davao or Butuan, but these are old sources and need local confirmation.
From the terminal, take a motorcycle or tricycle to PAMO (IPAS Complex, Mambalili village).
Rent a pumpboat at the wharf; it is about 2 hours to Lake Panlabuhan.
Some travel accounts also describe an overland route via Loreto, but road conditions and fares are outdated, so confirm the latest information.

Water levels in the marsh rise in months of heavy rain, and the scenery of the channels and lakes changes with them. Travel accounts name November to March, when migratory birds arrive, as the best time.
However, eastern Mindanao has no sharply defined wet and dry seasons and it can rain between December and February, so confirm boat operations and water levels with PAMO just before you leave.

The most common lodging is a cottage in the Panlabuhan floating village. The provincial program is a 1-night stay with lunch, dinner and breakfast in the village, and many accounts say the food centers on local dishes and freshwater fish. Confirm whether meals are included and what is served when you book.

Facilities are simple, so bring a mosquito net, a portable charger, personal toiletries and drinking water. Bunawan and Butuan have more regular accommodation, so you could also stay a night in Butuan and leave at dawn. Names and prices change, so check recent reviews on a map app.

In a floating village you cannot expect electricity or Wi-Fi, and nights are quiet and dark. Many visitors say this is the charm of the trip, not an inconvenience. On a clear evening, talk with the villagers and listen to their stories. Families with children should consider the boat travel time and mosquito protection beforehand.
Contact PAMO (hotline 09308044113 or email) or the provincial tourism office in advance to confirm your schedule.
Splitting a boat among a group lowers the cost per person. The rental is per boat, so going alone is expensive.
Before entering the Manobo community, ask PAMO about the panawagtawag ritual and photography etiquette.
Bring sunscreen, a hat, a rain jacket, a waterproof bag, mosquito repellent and spare clothes.
Mobile signal is weak in many places, so carry cash and an offline map.
Wear a life jacket on the boat and avoid traveling after sunset.
This is bird and crocodile habitat, so do not leave trash and do not put your hands in the water.
The environmental orientation at the sanctuary gate explains the rules, so listen carefully and ask the staff about anything you wonder about.
Small gifts such as rice or snacks for the Manobo community are welcome, but ask PAMO first what is needed.
This is a water area, so life jackets and compliance with sanctuary rules are mandatory, and fees and operations must be confirmed with PAMO just before departure.
This is crocodile habitat. Avoid swimming in the lake or dipping your hands and feet at the water's edge.
Use waterproof pouches so belongings do not fall into the water from boats and floating houses.
Heavy rain raises the water level and can change your plans. Check the latest announcements.
This is an indigenous village, so do not photograph the inside of homes or people without permission.
Fees differ between sources. Check receipts or the fee list on site.
A city that serves as an overland base, with museums and archaeological sites worth visiting before or after your marsh trip.
Mindanao's largest city and another gateway from a different direction. The overland trip to Bunawan can be long, so confirm the figure of around
3 hours
locally.
A clear, deep blue-green spring in Surigao del Sur that some travelers combine with Agusan in one itinerary.
